doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Accompanying singers at Birdland and playing in all keys
summary: At Birdland he backed many singers between Coltrane's quartet and Horace Silver's quintet sets, which sharpened his accompanying and transposing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Johnny Hartman, I played with Irene Reid, I had all the singing gigs from Birdland so consequently I was always on the scene. See it would be three bands. John Coltrane Quartet, Benny Carter Trio with Harold Mabern and Ron Carter and Roy McCurdy or Bill Lee and Roy McCurdy. Then I’d take a break then the Horace Silver Quintet. So that went on for years you know. So that really kind of tightened up my accompanying skills because I had expertise in playing for singers, and know how to treat this singer differently from that. If this singer was behind the beat and I felt I needed to pull her up I’d do something to enhance the beat, you know what I’m saying.
Yeah. And you learned a lot of different keys, too, I would imagine.

Yes, playing all the keys. Especially the female singers because say for example if they’re singing “Lush Life,” they’re not singing in D flat it’s too low. They’ve got to be singing maybe in the key of E, A or B. So you’ve got to really learn how to transpose. Oh yeah. You have to play in all the keys you know.
